results.answer: 3M's FY2018 capital expenditure was $1,577 million. This is the purchases of property, plant and equipment line (shown as an outflow of $(1,577) million) in the 2018 cash flow data. I took it from the free cash flow table in the MD&A and did not open the formal cash flow statement itself.

3M's net property, plant and equipment at year-end FY2018 was about $8.738 billion (roughly $8.7 billion). The balance sheet shows gross PP&E of $24,873 million less accumulated depreciation of $16,135 million, which gives $8,738 million.

No, 3M is only moderately capital-intensive, and not heavily so. In FY2022, 3M spent $1,749M on PP&E, which is about 5.1% of net sales of $34,229M. Depreciation and amortization was $1,831M, about 5.3% of sales. Net PP&E was $9,178M, about 27% of sales. Capex was about 31% of operating cash flow of $5,591M. 3M guides to about $1.5–1.8B of capex for 2023. These are moderate levels for a diversified industrial manufacturer, well below those of asset-heavy businesses.

Operating margin is a useful metric for 3M, which uses it as a primary segment performance measure. It fell 1.7 points, from 20.8% in 2021 to 19.1% in 2022. Special items were the largest driver: net significant-litigation costs (Combat Arms Earplugs and PFAS at Zwijndrecht) of 6.7 points, PFAS exit costs of 2.4, Russia exit charges of 0.3, divestiture costs of 0.2 and divestiture-related restructuring of 0.1. These were largely offset by an 8.0-point gain from the Food Safety divestiture. Excluding special items, margin slipped from 22.2% to 20.8%. Raw material and logistics inflation cost 2.4 points, and lower disposable respirator demand cost 0.3 points. Pricing, spending discipline and restructuring, net of supply-chain headwinds, added 1.3 points. By expense line, cost of sales rose 3.0 points of sales to 56.2% and SG&A rose 6.1 points to 26.5%. R&D fell 0.2 points to 5.4%, and goodwill impairment added 0.8 points.

The Consumer segment dragged down 3M's 2022 growth. Excluding M&A (acquisitions and divestitures), it was the only segment with negative organic sales growth, at -0.9%. The other segments grew organically: Safety and Industrial +1.0%, Transportation and Electronics +1.2%, and Health Care +3.2%. Total company organic growth was +1.2%.

The quick ratio is relevant, and it points to a somewhat weak liquidity profile rather than a clearly healthy one. At June 30, 2023, 3M's quick assets were cash of $4,258M, current marketable securities of $56M and receivables of $4,947M, which total $9,261M. Current liabilities were $10,936M, so the quick ratio is about 0.85. That is below 1.0, meaning quick assets don't fully cover current liabilities. The current ratio of 15,754/10,936 is about 1.44, which is helped by $5,280M of inventory, so liquidity is adequate but not strong on a quick basis.

As of 3M's Q2 2023 10-Q (quarter ended June 30, 2023), three debt securities are registered on a national securities exchange, all on the New York Stock Exchange: 1.500% Notes due 2026 (MMM26), 1.750% Notes due 2030 (MMM30) and 1.500% Notes due 2031 (MMM31). The cover page lists them under Section 12(b) alongside the common stock (NYSE and Chicago Stock Exchange).

Yes, through the filings in the library (FY2015–FY2022 10-Ks and a 2023 10-Q), 3M's dividend is stable and rising. It has paid dividends since 1916. Cash dividends per share rose from $4.10 in 2015 to $4.44 in 2016, $4.70 in 2017, $5.44 in 2018, $5.76 in 2019 and $5.88 in 2020. The FY2022 10-K says the February 2023 dividend of $1.50 per quarter ($6.00 annualized) was a 1% increase and the 65th consecutive year of increases. Q2 2023 dividends were $1.50, against $1.49 a year earlier. I did not find any filing covering a later dividend change.
FY2019 fixed asset turnover ≈ 24.26. Revenue of $6,489M divided by average PP&E of $267.5M, which is the average of $253M at 2019 and $282M at 2018.

The 3-year average capex as a % of revenue for FY2017–FY2019 is about 1.9%. Capex was $155M on revenue of $7,017M in 2017 (2.21%), $131M on $7,500M in 2018 (1.75%), and $116M on $6,489M in 2019 (1.79%). The average of those three ratios is about 1.92%.
FY2015 operating cash flow ratio ≈ 0.66. Cash from operations was $1,469,502K and total current liabilities were $2,213,556K at Nov 27, 2015, so the ratio is 1,469,502 / 2,213,556 ≈ 0.66.
Adobe's GAAP operating income rose about 65.4% year over year, from $903.095M in FY2015 to $1,493.602M in FY2016. The calculation is (1,493,602 − 903,095) / 903,095 = 65.4%.

Adobe's FY2017 operating cash flow ratio is about 0.83. Net cash provided by operating activities was $2,912,853K and total current liabilities were $3,527,457K, so the ratio is 2,912,853 / 3,527,457 = 0.826, which rounds to 0.83.

No, not in FY2022. Operating margin is a useful metric for Adobe, and it fell in FY2022 after rising in FY2021. It was 34.6% in FY2022 (operating income $6,098M on revenue $17,606M), down from 36.8% in FY2021 ($5,802M on $15,785M) and up from 32.9% in FY2020 ($4,237M on $12,868M). Operating income grew about 5% in FY2022 while revenue grew about 12%, because operating expenses rose faster than gross profit (R&D, sales and marketing, and G&A all grew about 14–18%). The two-year picture from FY2020 is up, but the latest year is a decline of about 2.2 percentage points.

Yes. Adobe's free cash flow conversion (OCF less capex, divided by net income) rose to about 156% in FY2022 from about 143% in FY2021 and 101% in FY2020. FY2022 FCF was $7,396M (OCF $7,838M less capex $442M) against net income of $4,756M. FY2021 FCF was $6,882M against net income of $4,822M. FY2020 FCF was $5,308M against net income of $5,260M.

0. AES's FY2022 Consolidated Statement of Operations has no restructuring cost line. Its line items include cost of sales, general and administrative expenses, interest expense, loss on extinguishment of debt, impairment expenses and others.

AES sold its inventory roughly 12 times in FY2022. Inventory turnover is total cost of sales divided by average inventory. Cost of sales was $10,069M. Average inventory was ($1,055M at 12/31/22 + $604M at 12/31/21) / 2 = $829.5M. That gives 10,069 / 829.5 ≈ 12.1x, or about 30 days of inventory. Using year-end inventory alone gives about 9.5x. Caveat: AES is a utility and power generator, and its cost of sales is mostly fuel, purchased power and operating costs, not goods held for resale. Its inventory is mainly fuel and spare parts, so the ratio is only a rough indicator and conventional inventory management is not very meaningful for the company.

AES's FY2022 ROA is about -1.42%. Net income (loss) was -$505M and total assets were $38,363M at FY2022 and $32,963M at FY2021, so average assets were $35,663M. ROA = -505 / 35,663 = -1.42%. This uses consolidated net loss. Using the loss attributable to The AES Corporation (-$546M) instead would give -1.53%.

FY2017 DPO ≈ 93.86 days. Average accounts payable is (25,309 + 34,616)/2 = 29,962.5. The change in inventory is 16,047 − 11,461 = 4,586. FY2017 cost of sales is 111,934, so the denominator is 111,934 + 4,586 = 116,520. DPO = 365 × 29,962.5 / 116,520 = 93.86.
Amazon's total net sales grew 30.8% from FY2016 to FY2017. Total net sales rose from $135,987M to $177,866M, and (177,866 − 135,987) / 135,987 = 30.8%.

Amazon's FY2019 net income attributable to shareholders was $11,588 million. The income statement shows no noncontrolling interest, so net income is the amount attributable to shareholders. It is income before taxes of $13,976M, less a $2,374M tax provision, less $14M of equity-method losses.

Amcor's net trade receivables at year end FY2020 (June 30, 2020) were $1,615.9 million, as shown on the consolidated balance sheet. The FY2021 10-K's note shows $1,616 million for the same date, rounded.

The 8-K (Item 8.01, Other Events) reported a substitution of issuers on Amcor's guaranteed senior notes. On June 30, 2022, Amcor Finance (USA), Inc. (the Former Issuer) and Amcor Flexibles North America, Inc. (the Substitute Issuer), both wholly-owned subsidiaries of Amcor plc, signed a Second Supplemental Indenture to the 2016 Indenture and a First Supplemental Indenture to the 2019 Indenture with Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas as trustee. These cover the 3.625% Guaranteed Senior Notes due 2026 and the 4.500% Guaranteed Senior Notes due 2028. The Substitute Issuer replaced the Former Issuer and assumed its covenants under the indentures. The supplemental indentures were filed as Exhibits 4.6 and 4.7 under Item 9.01.

The quick ratio improved. Using (cash + trade receivables) / current liabilities, it rose from about 0.53 in FY2022 ((775+1,935)/5,103) to about 0.57 in FY2023 ((689+1,875)/4,476). Current liabilities fell by more than cash and receivables did, mainly because trade payables dropped from 3,073 to 2,690. The ratio is below 1.0 in both years, which is normal for a large packaging manufacturer with big inventories and trade payables.

Amcor made three small acquisitions in FY2023 and none that the 10-Ks describe in FY2022 or FY2021. FY2023 (year ended June 30, 2023), all in the Flexibles segment: (1) On Aug 1, 2022, it bought 100% of a Czech Republic flexible packaging plant (DGPack s.r.o.) for $59M, including $23M of goodwill. (2) On Mar 17, 2023, it bought a medical device packaging site in Shanghai, China for $60M, including $20M of contingent consideration and $39M of goodwill. (3) On May 31, 2023, it bought a New Zealand maker of automated protein packaging machines for $45M, including $13M of contingent consideration and $36M of goodwill. FY2022: the Acquisitions and Divestitures note covers only divestitures, namely non-core Flexibles assets (a $10M expense). FY2021: the note also covers only divestitures, namely a European hospital supplies business, businesses in India and Argentina, and the AMVIG stake. The last major acquisition shown in these notes is Bemis, completed June 11, 2019 (FY2019) for about $5.23B in equity.

Amcor primarily operates in the packaging industry. It develops and produces flexible packaging, rigid packaging containers, specialty cartons and closures. Its two reportable segments are Flexibles and Rigid Packaging. It sells mainly to the food, beverage, pharmaceutical, medical device, home and personal care, and other consumer goods end markets. This comes from the FY2023 10-K, Note 1.

No. Amcor's gross margin did not improve in FY2023. It fell to 18.5% from 19.4% in FY2022, and FY2022 was itself down from 21.2% in FY2021. Gross profit dropped $95M (3%) to $2,725M from $2,820M. The filing attributes the margin decline mainly to the pass-through of higher raw material costs, which inflates sales without adding profit and so dilutes the percentage, plus the effect of disposed operations. On that basis gross margin % is a distorted metric for Amcor. Excluding currency and disposals, gross profit rose $56M on favorable operating cost performance, so dollar profitability held up better than the margin % suggests.

As of December 31, 2022 (Q2 FY2023), Amcor's restructuring liability was $93 million. It was made up of $81M employee costs, $2M fixed-asset-related costs and $10M other costs. It is a restructuring plan accrual, mainly for Russia-Ukraine conflict restructuring activities. It also includes the remaining balance from the 2019 Bemis integration plan, which was substantially completed at the end of FY2022. The liability fell from $118M at June 30, 2022, after $25M cash paid, $2M net charges and $2M reversals. Most of it is expected to be paid within 12 months. It is recorded in other current and non-current liabilities.

Amcor's adjusted (non-GAAP) EBITDA for fiscal 2023 (twelve months ended June 30, 2023) was $2,018 million. It is down from $2,117 million in fiscal 2022. The reconciliation starts from EBITDA of $2,080 million and adjusts for hyperinflation, the Russia-Ukraine gain and other items.

Excluding FX (−$426M), raw material pass-through (+$776M) and disposed/ceased operations (−$207M), Amcor's FY2023 net sales rose only $7 million, or about 0%. Reported sales were $14,694M against $14,544M in FY2022, up $150M or 1%. The underlying change reflects price/mix of +3% and volume of −3%.
AMD's FY2015 D&A margin is about 4.2%. D&A from the cash flow statement was $167M and net revenue from the income statement was $3,991M, so 167/3,991 = 4.18%.

Yes. AMD's FY22 quick ratio is about 1.57, from (cash $4,835M + short-term investments $1,020M + accounts receivable $4,126M = $9,981M) divided by current liabilities of $6,369M. A ratio above 1.0 means its most liquid assets cover short-term obligations without selling inventory ($3,771M). The quick ratio is a relevant measure here, and AMD's liquidity is healthy.

In FY22 AMD sold: (1) client processors (Ryzen, Ryzen PRO, Threadripper, Threadripper PRO, Athlon, Athlon PRO, PRO A-Series) for desktop and notebook PCs; (2) graphics: Radeon for consumer, Radeon PRO for professional, and Radeon Instinct, Radeon PRO V-series and AMD Instinct accelerators for data centers, plus chipsets; (3) EPYC server processors; (4) embedded processors (Athlon, Geode, Ryzen, EPYC, R-Series and G-Series) and AMD Embedded Radeon graphics; (5) Xilinx FPGAs (Virtex, Kintex, Artix, Spartan); (6) Adaptive SoCs (Zynq, Versal, plus Vitis and Vivado tools); and (7) Alveo compute and network acceleration boards. This comes from the product brand descriptions in the FY22 10-K.

AMD's FY22 net revenue rose 44% to $23.6B from $16.4B in FY21. Data Center revenue rose 64% (to $6,043M from $3,694M), mainly on higher EPYC server processor sales. Gaming rose 21% (to $6,805M from $5,607M) on higher semi-custom sales. Embedded rose to $4,552M from $246M because Xilinx embedded sales were included after the acquisition. Client revenue fell 10% (to $6,201M from $6,887M) on lower processor shipments, a weak PC market and inventory correction, which partly offset the growth.

Operating margin fell sharply, from about 22% in FY21 to about 5% in FY22. I computed both figures from the income statement lines. FY22 operating income was about $1,264M on $23,601M revenue (10,603 − 5,005 − 2,336 − 2,100 + 102), or 5.4%. FY21 operating income was about $3,648M on $16,434M revenue (7,929 − 2,845 − 1,448 + 12), or 22.2%. The main driver was the Xilinx acquisition in February 2022. It added $1,448M of amortization of acquisition-related intangibles in cost of sales and $2,100M in operating expenses, and neither existed in 2021. That lowered gross margin from 48% to 45%. R&D rose from $2,845M to $5,005M and marketing, general and administrative from $1,448M to $2,336M. The 'All Other' segment's $5.0B operating loss consisted mainly of $3.5B of acquisition amortization, $1.1B of stock-based compensation and $452M of acquisition-related costs. Embedded segment operating income rose to $2.3B from $44M because Xilinx revenue was included. Operating margin is still a usable metric, but the GAAP figure is distorted by these non-cash acquisition charges. Segment operating income, which excludes them, shows the underlying business more clearly.

Operating activities brought in the most cash for AMD in FY22, at $3,565M. Investing activities provided $1,999M and financing activities used $3,264M. Operating cash flow was therefore the largest of the three.
Data Center. Its sales rose about 63.6%, from $3,694M in FY21 to $6,043M in FY22. Gaming rose about 21.4% ($5,607M to $6,805M) and Client fell about 10% ($6,887M to $6,201M). Embedded is excluded.

Yes. AMD's FY22 10-K reports one major customer (Customer A) at 16% of consolidated net revenue in 2022, up from 14% in 2021. Its sales were from the Gaming segment. Customer B was 11% in 2021 but below 10% in 2022. The 10-K also reports that one customer made up about 18% of accounts receivable at December 31, 2022.

None. As of the FY2022 10-K (year ended December 31, 2022), the only security American Express Company registered under Section 12(b) is its Common Shares (par value $0.20 per share), ticker AXP, listed on the New York Stock Exchange. No debt securities are listed under its name. Section 12(g) registration is 'None'.

As of 2022, American Express reports its geographic operations in four regions: the United States, EMEA (Europe, the Middle East and Africa), APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand), and LACC (Latin America, Canada and the Caribbean). The United States is by far the largest, with $41,396M of the $52,862M consolidated 2022 revenue net of interest expense. EMEA contributed $4,871M, APAC $3,835M and LACC $2,917M. A further -$157M is in Other Unallocated.

Not on a conventional basis. AMEX's income statement has no operating income line. Interest expense is a funding cost and provisions for credit losses are an operating cost, so a standard operating margin isn't a clean metric for a card issuer and lender. Pretax margin (pretax income / total revenues net of interest expense) is a reasonable proxy. It was 18.1% in 2022 (9,585 / 52,862), down from 25.2% in 2021 (10,689 / 42,380), though up from 11.9% in 2020 (4,296 / 36,087). Margin therefore did not improve in 2022. Revenue grew about 25%, but provisions for credit losses swung from a (1,419) million reserve release in 2021 to a 2,182 million expense, and total expenses rose 24% to 41,095 million. Pretax income fell about 10%, so the 2022 profile is a decline from the 2021 peak.

Gross margin isn't a useful metric for American Express. It is a financial services company, and its income statement has no cost of goods sold or gross profit line. Revenue is reported as total revenues net of interest expense, and interest expense is a financing cost, not a cost of goods sold. The better measures are revenue growth, net interest income and pretax income. I did not read the expense or pretax income pages, so I can't say what drove margins at that level. The revenue drivers for FY2022 are below. Total revenues net of interest expense rose 25% to $52,862M from $42,380M. Discount revenue rose $6,176M (25%) on a 23% increase in billed business. Net card fees rose 17%, driven by premium card growth. Service fees and other revenue rose 36%, driven by foreign exchange revenues, travel commissions and delinquency fees. Interest income rose 40% to $12,658M on higher average loan balances and rates. Interest expense more than doubled to $2,763M from $1,283M on higher rates paid on deposits and debt. Net interest income rose 28% to $9,895M.

American Express's effective tax rate fell by 3.0 percentage points, from 24.6% in FY2021 to 21.6% in FY2022. The 10-K attributes the drop mainly to discrete tax benefits in 2022 from the resolution of prior-year tax items.

Customer deposits were American Express's largest liability at December 31, 2022, at $110,239 million. That is about 54% of total liabilities of $203,643 million. The next largest were long-term debt at $42,573 million and other liabilities at $37,350 million.

Yes. American Express grew its card base in 2022 despite attrition, with total cards-in-force rising 10% to 133.3 million from 121.7 million in 2021. Proprietary cards-in-force rose 7% to 76.7 million from 71.4 million, and proprietary basic cards-in-force rose 8% to 59.1 million from 54.7 million. The 10-K tables show net growth but do not give a specific retention or attrition rate.
American Water Works paid about $0.389 billion in cash dividends in FY2020. The Consolidated Statement of Cash Flows shows 'Dividends paid' of $(389) million for 2020, up from $353 million in 2019.

American Water Works' FY2021 unadjusted EBITDA is about $1,832 million. That is operating income of $1,196M from the income statement plus depreciation and amortization of $636M from the cash flow statement.

No. American Water Works had negative working capital at FY2022 year-end (Dec 31, 2022). Total current assets were $1,250M and total current liabilities were $2,811M, so working capital was about -$1,561M (current ratio about 0.44). Working capital is of limited use for this company because it is a capital-intensive regulated utility. It funds long-lived infrastructure with short-term debt of $1,175M and the current portion of long-term debt of $281M, and it relies on regulated, recurring cash flows and capital-market access. A negative figure therefore does not signal distress.

About 2.8%. Net margin (net earnings attributable to Best Buy shareholders ÷ revenue) was 3.12% for FY2017 ($1,228M / $39,403M), 2.27% for FY2016 ($897M / $39,528M) and 3.06% for FY2015 ($1,233M / $40,339M). Their average is about 2.81%. I took FY2015–FY2017 as the three fiscal years ended January 31, 2015, January 30, 2016 and January 28, 2017.
Best Buy's merchandise inventories were $5,409 million at fiscal year end February 2, 2019 (FY2019). This is the figure on the Consolidated Balance Sheet, up from $5,209 million a year earlier.

Yes. Best Buy's gross margin is a relevant metric and has been consistent. It has stayed in a narrow band of about 21.4%–24.0% and moved by no more than about 1.1 percentage points in any year. The reported consolidated gross profit rates are: FY2017 24.0%, FY2018 23.4%, FY2019 23.2%, FY2020 23.0%, FY2021 22.4%, FY2022 22.5% and FY2023 21.4%. The largest annual change was the 1.1-point drop in FY2023, caused by lower product margins and Totaltech membership costs. The FY2022–FY2023 changes are well inside the roughly 2% threshold. One caveat from the filing: Best Buy's gross profit rate may not be comparable to other retailers' because companies classify supply chain costs differently between cost of sales and SG&A.

FY2023: no acquisitions are disclosed in the FY2023 10-K. Its acquisitions note covers only the two FY2022 deals. FY2022: Best Buy bought Current Health Ltd., a care-at-home technology platform, on Nov 2, 2021 for $389M net cash, including $351M of goodwill. It also bought Two Peaks, LLC d/b/a Yardbird Furniture, a direct-to-consumer outdoor furniture company, on Nov 4, 2021 for $79M net cash, including $47M of goodwill. FY2021: no acquisitions are disclosed in the FY2021 10-K. Its acquisitions note lists only earlier deals: BioSensics ($20M, Aug 2019) and CST ($125M, May 2019), both in FY2020, and GreatCall ($787M, Oct 2018) in FY2019.

Operating activities were the best. In FY2023 (year ended Jan 28, 2023) Best Buy generated $1,824M of cash from operations. Investing used $962M and financing used $1,806M, so operations was the only one of the three that brought in cash.

Yes. Assuming the question is about Best Buy (the library has Q2 FY2024 filings for other companies too, such as Salesforce and Ulta, which I did not check), cash and cash equivalents fell from $1,874 million at January 28, 2023 (end of FY2023) to $1,093 million at July 29, 2023 (end of Q2 FY2024). That is a drop of $781 million, or about 41.7%.

Yes, the store count fell. Domestic stores were 969 at the end of Q2 FY2024, against 982 at the end of Q2 FY2023, a decrease of 13. Best Buy-branded domestic stores went from 930 to 907. Outlet Centers rose from 18 to 20, Pacific Sales fell from 21 to 20, and Yardbird rose from 13 to 22. International (Canada) stores were 160 at the end of both quarters, so there was no change there. Best Buy-branded Canada stores went from 127 to 128, offset by Best Buy Mobile going from 33 to 32. Combining the two segments gives 1,129 at Q2 FY2024 against 1,142 at Q2 FY2023, a decrease of 13.

Computing and Mobile Phones was the top category in the Domestic segment in Q2 FY2024 (quarter ended July 29, 2023). It made up 41% of Domestic revenue, which was $8,890M, so roughly $3.6B. That is ahead of Consumer Electronics at 30%, Appliances at 16%, Entertainment at 6%, Services at 6% and Other at 1%. Its comparable sales fell 6.4%.
Block's (Square's) FY2016 working capital ratio is about 1.73. Total current assets were $1,001,425K and total current liabilities were $577,464K, so 1,001,425 / 577,464 ≈ 1.73.
Block's total net revenue grew 101.5% from FY2019 to FY2020. Total net revenue rose from $4,713,500K in FY2019 to $9,497,578K in FY2020, and 9,497,578 / 4,713,500 − 1 ≈ 101.5%.

Block generated about $381.6 million in net cash provided by operating activities in FY2020 ($381,603 thousand). This is the 2020 figure in the cash flow table of Block's FY2020 10-K, which compares it with $465.7 million for 2019. I did not open the page to confirm the column headers, and I assumed the first column is 2020.

Boeing's net property, plant and equipment at December 31, 2018 was $12,645 million. This is the "Property, plant and equipment, net" line on the Consolidated Statements of Financial Position (it was $12,672 million at year-end 2017).

Yes. Three of Boeing's four segments each exceeded 20% of FY2022 total revenue of $66,608M. Commercial Airplanes was $25,867M (~38.8%), Defense, Space & Security was $23,162M (~34.8%), and Global Services was $17,611M (~26.4%). Boeing Capital ($199M, ~0.3%) did not.

Yes. Boeing's FY2022 10-K (Note 21) names two material ongoing matters. (1) Multiple lawsuits from the Lion Air 610 (Oct 2018) and Ethiopian Airlines 302 (Mar 2019) 737 MAX accidents are still pending. The 2021 DOJ Deferred Prosecution Agreement and a shareholder derivative settlement ($219M received in Q2 2022) are resolved. So is the SEC investigation (September 2022 settlement, $200M civil penalty paid October 2022). Boeing cannot reasonably estimate any loss not covered by insurance on the remaining suits. (2) Embraer is disputing Boeing's 2020 termination of the planned $4.2B commercial aircraft joint venture. That dispute is in arbitration, with completion expected in late 2023 or early 2024, and no loss range can be estimated. Boeing also says various other proceedings and government investigations are pending, but it does not expect them to be material.

Yes, modestly. Gross margin is usable here, though it is a limited metric. Boeing reports no gross profit line, so I derived it as total revenues minus total costs and expenses. It was about 5.3% in FY2022 (3,502 on 66,608 revenue). That compares with about 4.8% in FY2021 (3,017 on 62,286) and about -9.8% in FY2020 (-5,685 on 58,158). The profile is improving from the 2020 trough, but margins remain thin. Boeing still posted an operating loss of $3.5B and a net loss of $5.1B in 2022 after G&A and R&D. Gross margin also leaves out large R&D and G&A costs, and long-term program accounting (reach-forward losses, estimate changes) distorts it. Operating margin and cash flow are therefore more informative for a company like this.

As of FY2022, Boeing's primary customers are commercial airlines worldwide and the U.S. government. Commercial Airplanes sells jets principally to the commercial airline industry, and a significant portion of revenue comes from a limited number of airlines. Defense, Space & Security and Global Services serve defense customers, mainly the U.S. government (with other non-U.S. government customers as well). Boeing Capital finances customers' purchases of Boeing products. I did not read a passage that explicitly lists the U.S. government as a primary customer. That part rests on the filing's description of BDS and BGS long-term contracts with the U.S. government and other customers (page 63, lines 1968-1973), which I saw only as a search snippet.

Yes. Boeing's business is exposed to cyclicality through its heavy dependence on commercial airlines. Its 10-K risk factors say "Historically, the airline industry has been cyclical and very competitive and has experienced significant profit swings." A downturn in the economy, the airline industry or customer finances could lead to fewer new orders, postponed or cancelled orders and payments, lower revenues, profitability and cash flows, and a smaller backlog. This language appears in the FY2022 10-K and in the other Boeing 10-Ks the search returned (FY2015–FY2021). I read only the FY2022 passage in full.

Boeing's FY2022 10-K gives these 2023 production-rate expectations. 737: it reached 31 per month in 2022 and expects further gradual increases in 2023, based on market demand and supply chain capacity. 787: it is producing at low rates now and expects to gradually return to 5 per month in 2023. 767: no change is stated; it is producing at a combined 3 per month. 777/777X: no change is stated; it is producing at a combined 3 per month, and 777X-9 production is paused during 2022 and 2023. 747: production ended in Q4 2022, with the last delivery expected in early 2023.

Boeing's effective tax rate was (0.6)% in FY2022, against 14.7% in FY2021, so it fell by about 15.3 percentage points. In 2022 Boeing booked income tax expense of $31M on a pre-tax loss of $5,022M, which gives a slightly negative rate. In 2021 it booked a tax benefit of $743M on a pre-tax loss of $5,033M. The main driver was the valuation allowance, which was $1,199M in 2022 and $512M in 2021.

No. J&J's FY2022 financials are those of a mature, stable company, not a high-growth one. Sales rose only 1.3% to $94.9B (from $93.8B), down from 13.6% growth in 2021. Gross margin is a usable metric for J&J, and it fell in FY2022. Computed from the income statement, it was about 67.3% in 2022 (sales $94,943M less cost of products sold $31,089M = $63,854M) against about 68.2% in 2021 ($93,775M less $29,855M = $63,920M). That is a decline of roughly 0.9 points. The 10-K says cost of products sold rose as a percent of sales because of: (1) one-time COVID-19 vaccine manufacturing exit costs; (2) currency impacts in the Pharmaceutical segment; and (3) commodity inflation in MedTech and Consumer Health. Supply chain benefits in Consumer Health partly offset these. Intangible asset amortization within cost of products sold was $4.3B in 2022 versus $4.7B in 2021. The margin is only a partial view of profitability. J&J's large R&D and SG&A spending, plus litigation and other items, also matter: pre-tax earnings fell from 24.3% to 22.9% of sales.

About $82.31 per common share. This is JPM's book value per share at March 31, 2021, which is common equity divided by shares outstanding. It assumes assets sell at book value and preferred equity is paid first. If goodwill and intangibles fetched nothing, the figure would be the tangible book value of about $66.56 per share.

Gross margin is not a relevant metric for JPM. As a bank, JPM has no cost of goods sold or gross profit line. Its income statement shows interest income and interest expense, which net to net interest income, plus noninterest revenue, giving total net revenue. Below that come provision for credit losses and noninterest expense. Interest expense is an operating cost of funding, not a cost of goods sold. Banks are usually assessed on net interest margin, efficiency ratio, ROE/ROTCE and credit costs instead. A gross margin figure would also not stay within about 2% year to year, because it would swing with interest rates. In Q1 2023, interest expense was $16,293M against $1,624M in Q1 2022, and net interest income rose to $20,711M from $13,872M. I did not compute a gross margin series, so this is a judgment about the metric's relevance, not a measured result.

Verizon's FY2022 quick ratio is about 0.54, which is below 1.0. That is computed as (cash $2,605M + net accounts receivable $24,506M = $27,111M) divided by total current liabilities of $50,171M. It is a stable, cash-generating telecom with recurring subscription revenue, and it routinely refinances debt (current liabilities include $9,963M of debt maturing within a year). Its current ratio is about 0.75 (37,857/50,171). Operating margin rose by about 0.2 percentage points, from 4.08% in FY2018 to 4.27% in FY2019. FY2018 is 20,437 / 500,343 = 4.08%, and FY2019 is 21,957 / 514,405 = 4.27%. The difference is about +0.18 points, which rounds to +0.2.

The FY2018–FY2020 average unadjusted EBITDA margin is about 6.2%. EBITDA is operating income plus cash-flow-statement D&A, divided by total revenues. FY2020: (20,568 + 10,987) / 523,964 = 6.02%. FY2019: (21,957 + 10,678) / 514,405 = 6.34%. FY2018: (20,437 + 10,529) / 500,343 = 6.19%. The three-year average is 6.185%, which rounds to 6.2%.
